chapters.title: Buyer, workflow, and economic unit
chapters.body:
### Start with the unit of work
A service becomes specific when it names one repeatable unit: a support ticket, a purchase record, or a participant handout. Write its trigger, input, current operator, output, and completion rule. A department is too large a unit for a first pilot. A single generated sentence is too small if it cannot finish an actual handoff. Use the fictional training provider throughout this course: the unit is one reviewed handout made from approved course notes.

### Separate three customers
The operator feels the friction, the operational owner is accountable for quality, and the budget owner can fund a change. An instructor may like your demo while the operations lead cannot provide source access and finance has not agreed to recurring costs. Draw three columns and put a named role in each. A single person may occupy multiple columns, but never infer authority from enthusiasm. Ask who accepts the deliverable and who maintains it after you leave.

### Score feasibility without hiding uncertainty
Use four gates before scoring attractiveness: permission to use representative inputs, an observable output standard, a reviewer with time, and a reversible fallback. Failure of a gate means investigate or decline. For opportunities that pass, compare monthly volume, minutes of avoidable work, cost of a wrong accepted output, and your familiarity with the workflow. Keep evidence and assumptions in separate fields. A score of four based on an assumption is not stronger evidence than a score of two based on observation.

### Worked opportunity comparison
Suppose course handouts occur 40 times a month, take 20 minutes each, and always receive instructor review. A payroll adjustment occurs 10 times, takes 8 minutes, and can move money. Even if payroll looks easier to automate technically, the first engagement has a more reversible draft boundary. Choose the handout workflow because you can observe review quality and stop before distribution. The decision is about the test you can run, not the most impressive demo.

### Write a falsifiable offer hypothesis
Use: “For [operator], we will test whether [bounded workflow] improves [observable measure], while [guardrail] stays within [limit], using [permitted inputs].” Add what would disprove it. For the training provider, a failed hypothesis might be that source notes are too incomplete for a reviewer to accept drafts without rewriting. That result should trigger source cleanup or a different service, rather than a stronger prompt.

### Practice record
Create rows for unit, operator, owner, authorizer, monthly volume, evidence source, unknown, and next test. Complete three candidate workflows. Select one and explain which missing fact could reverse your decision. Your output is a defensible opportunity choice; it is not evidence that someone will buy it.

chapters.title: Define the Outcome Before You Choose the Output
chapters.body:
## Output Is Not Outcome

“Build an incident assistant” names an output. It does not say who needs it, what becomes better, or what must remain safe.

An outcome frame says:

> When a production alert arrives, the on-call engineer identifies the failing service and a safe next action within two minutes, while diagnosis remains read-only and auditable.

That sentence can be satisfied by software, a runbook, a data repair, or a smaller interface change. It keeps the team attached to the result rather than the first artifact someone imagined.

## The Six-Part Frame

| Part | Question |
|---|---|
| User | Who experiences the problem directly? |
| Situation | When and where does it occur? |
| Current behavior | What happens today, including workarounds? |
| Desired outcome | What observable state should improve? |
| Constraints | Which safety, policy, cost, or compatibility limits are fixed? |
| Non-goals | What tempting adjacent work is excluded? |

**System flow**

- User and situation → Current behavior
- Desired outcome
- Constraints
- Non-goals
- Evidence question

## Find Solution Leakage

Outcome statements leak solutions when they contain a product form, interface, model choice, framework, or architecture that has not been earned by evidence.

- “Users receive a weekly AI summary” leaks the summary and cadence.
- “Users understand account changes before approval” states the result.
- “Deploy a vector database” leaks infrastructure.
- “Relevant policy evidence is available during review” states a capability.

Constraints can name technology when compatibility truly fixes it. Record why it is fixed.

## Constraints Protect the Outcome

Constraints are not implementation details. They are part of the real-world goal:

- no production writes during diagnosis;
- response within the incident time budget;
- existing audit events remain authoritative;
- no new runtime dependency;
- accessibility behavior remains intact.

A build that reaches the outcome by violating a constraint has not reached the outcome.

## Non-Goals Create a Boundary

Non-goals prevent a useful slice from turning into a platform. Good non-goals are concrete enough to reject work:

- no automatic remediation;
- no new alert-routing system;
- no replacement of the incident commander;
- no historical analytics in this slice.

chapters.title: Map Assumptions and Resolve the Riskiest One First
chapters.body:
## Every Build Contains Bets

An incident tool may depend on all of these being true:

- alert context contains enough information to identify a service;
- engineers trust a recommendation they did not derive themselves;
- the desired response time matters operationally;
- required data can be accessed without unsafe authority;
- the workflow happens often enough to justify maintenance.

These are not implementation tasks. They are conditions for the build to be valuable, usable, feasible, and safe.

## Assumption Classes

| Class | Question |
|---|---|
| Value | Will the outcome matter enough? |
| Usability | Can the user understand and act on it? |
| Feasibility | Can the system produce it with available data and constraints? |
| Viability | Can the organization sustain cost, ownership, and operation? |
| Safety | Can it fail without unacceptable consequence? |

Write assumptions as falsifiable statements. “The feature is useful” cannot be tested. “Eight of ten on-call engineers identify the correct service faster with the read-only result” can.

## Risk Is Not One Number

The lab uses three dimensions from one to five:

- **Impact:** damage if the assumption is false.
- **Uncertainty:** weakness of current evidence.
- **Irreversibility:** cost of learning after commitment.

The example score multiplies impact and uncertainty, then adds irreversibility. The formula is not universal. Its purpose is to force the team to state why one unknown should be resolved before another.

**System flow**

- Assumptions → Score risk
- Highest open risk
- Cheapest decisive experiment
- Bounded build
- Reframe or stop

## Design an Experiment, Not a Confirmation Ritual

A useful test has:

- a claim that could be false;
- a population or realistic sample;
- an observable result;
- a threshold decided before the result;
- a next decision for pass, fail, and ambiguous evidence.

Avoid tests that only demonstrate that the team can build the idea.

## Reversibility Changes Order

High-consequence, irreversible choices need earlier evidence. A read-only replay can precede a production integration. A temporary adapter can precede a data migration. A human-approved recommendation can precede automatic action.

The shape of the build should follow the shape of uncertainty.

chapters.title: Map Assumptions and Resolve the Riskiest One First · implementation walkthrough
chapters.body:
Read the control flow before running or changing it. This pinned teaching implementation illustrates the chapter; source-specific dependencies and fixtures are named in its code. The short exercise in the Exercise tab is a separate standard-library practice.

```python
# Lesson program: ranks assumptions and selects the next risk-reducing experiment.
# Lesson: phases/14-agent-engineering/49-map-assumptions-and-risk/docs/en.md
# Canonical source: Boehm, Spiral Model, DOI 10.1145/12944.12948.
# Canonical source: Dardenne et al., Goal-Directed Requirements Acquisition.
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Assumption:
    statement: str
    impact: int
    uncertainty: int
    irreversibility: int
    test: str
    evidence: str = ""


def risk_score(item: Assumption) -> int:
    for value in (item.impact, item.uncertainty, item.irreversibility):
        if value not in range(1, 6):
            raise ValueError("risk dimensions must be integers from one to five")
    return item.impact * item.uncertainty + item.irreversibility


def prioritize(items: list[Assumption]) -> list[dict]:
    ranked = sorted(items, key=lambda item: (-risk_score(item), item.statement))
    return [{**asdict(item), "risk_score": risk_score(item), "status": "tested" if item.evidence else "open"} for item in ranked]


def next_experiment(items: list[Assumption]) -> Assumption | None:
    open_items = [item for item in items if not item.evidence]
    return max(open_items, key=risk_score, default=None)


def example() -> list[Assumption]:
    return [
        Assumption("Engineers can identify the right service from alert context", 5, 5, 2, "Replay ten incidents with a read-only prototype"),
        Assumption("Two-minute diagnosis matters", 4, 2, 1, "Interview five incident commanders", "four of five confirmed"),
        Assumption("Automatic remediation is acceptable", 5, 4, 5, "Do not automate; test approval workflow first"),
    ]


def main() -> None:
    output = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "outputs" / "assumption-map.json"
    output.write_text(json.dumps(prioritize(example()), indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

chapters.title: Apply it: Choose a workflow and a buyer
chapters.body:
## The engineering or business decision

A service offer connects a specific buyer to a recurring problem you can credibly address. “I build AI agents” describes a method, not a customer outcome. Choose a workflow you understand well enough to observe its inputs, handoffs, exceptions, and cost of mistakes. Identify who experiences the pain, who approves the work, and who will use the result; these may be three different people.

Start with a low-risk read-only or draft workflow. Do not promise autonomous decisions, regulated advice, or operational savings before measuring the process. Your first goal is to establish whether the problem is frequent, costly enough to matter, and accessible with permissioned data. A simulated client is sufficient for the program exercises.

## Worked example

A fictional training provider spends hours turning approved course notes into participant handouts. The operations lead owns the process; instructors review factual content; finance approves spending. Your offer could be a draft-and-review workflow for one course format, rather than “AI transformation for the whole company.”

## Build it yourself

1. Choose three familiar industries and one recurring workflow in each.
2. Map user, operational owner, budget owner, and reviewer for each workflow.
3. Score frequency, data access, error cost, and your relevant experience using stated assumptions.
4. Select one simulated client and write a narrow problem hypothesis.

## Break it deliberately

The person who likes your demo cannot authorize data access or budget. Revise your discovery plan to involve the missing decision maker.

## Acceptance checks

- The offer names a buyer and an end user.
- The problem is described independently of a tool.
- Important unknowns are labeled as hypotheses.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/opportunity-brief.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

lessons.title: Conduct discovery with evidence
lessons.content:
# Conduct discovery with evidence

## Discovery interviews and evidence synthesis

### Observe the work before proposing a solution
A discovery interview should reconstruct a recent completed case. Start with “Show me the last handout you prepared.” Ask which source arrived, how the operator decided what to include, which correction took longest, who approved it, and what happened after approval. Follow the artifact through the workflow. Asking whether AI would help invites a prediction; observing a recent correction gives you evidence.

### Use an interview sequence
Begin with context and permission. Move to a specific recent example. Trace its normal path. Ask for an exception and its consequence. Identify the people and systems involved. Finish by summarizing your understanding and asking what you missed. Keep questions neutral: “What happens when a note is incomplete?” gives more information than “Would automatic completion solve missing notes?” The latter hides the possibility that completing missing information is unacceptable.

### Keep an evidence ledger
Use four columns: observation, interpretation, assumption, and unresolved question. “The instructor corrected three objectives in the example” is an observation. “Objectives are the largest source of rework” is an interpretation requiring more examples. “This happens every week” is an assumption until you inspect records or hear a supported account. Write a source and date beside each observation. Mark role-play data as simulated.

### Resolve disagreement instead of averaging it
An operator says review takes ten minutes; a manager says two. Both can be describing different intervals. Ask each to identify start and end events. One may count source lookup while the other measures only approval clicks. Define a common timing rule, observe a case, and keep the disagreement in the record until resolved. Do not average incompatible measurements into a confident six-minute baseline.

### Handle access as a separate decision
Permission to discuss a document is not permission to upload it. Use a redacted or synthetic sample during initial discovery. Record who can authorize production access, which fields can leave the organization, and whether provider processing is permitted. If those answers are missing, your next deliverable may be a data-access map rather than a prototype.

### Interview exercise
Role-play an operator who wants faster drafts and an instructor whose main problem is factual errors. Ask eight questions without proposing a product. Produce a current-state map, three observations, two contradictions, one disconfirming finding, and a follow-up test. A good discovery summary can recommend no build when the bottleneck is approval ownership rather than text generation.

## Discover the Workflow People Actually Perform

## Start with the Current System

Do not begin by asking what features people want. Begin by reconstructing what happens now.

For each step, record:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Actor | On-call engineer |
| Trigger | Production alert arrives |
| Action | Opens alert, then searches dashboards |
| Input | Alert payload and deployment record |
| Output | Candidate service and owner |
| Friction | Context switching across three tools |
| Authority | Incident commander approves a write |
| Evidence | Screen recording, incident log, runbook |

The workflow is larger than the screen. It includes waiting, copy-paste, side channels, approval, error recovery, and the steps people have stopped noticing.

## Evidence Has Strength

Use a simple evidence ladder:

1. **Direct behavior:** observation, trace, recording, or system event.
2. **Artifact:** ticket, runbook, log, form, or completed output.
3. **Reported behavior:** a person describes what they do.
4. **Inference:** the team concludes what probably happens.

All four can be useful. Only the first two prove current behavior directly. Label the rest so confidence does not silently inflate.

**System flow**

- Trigger → Actor action
- Handoff
- Next actor action
- Outcome
- Direct evidence
- Artifact
- Reported behavior

## Search for Four Things

- **Friction:** repeated effort, delay, re-entry, or recovery.
- **Hidden state:** facts carried in memory, chat, or personal notes.
- **Authority:** the person or system allowed to make a consequential change.
- **Exceptions:** the case where the normal workflow stops being normal.

AI features often fail at handoffs and exceptions because the happy path was the only path shaped.

## Do Not Average Away Disagreement

Two users can perform different workflows for good reasons. Preserve the variants until you understand whether they represent:

- different roles;
- different risk levels;
- legacy and current process;
- expertise differences;
- a genuine policy disagreement.

An averaged workflow can describe nobody.

## Discover the Workflow People Actually Perform · implementation walkthrough

Read the control flow before running or changing it. This pinned teaching implementation illustrates the chapter; source-specific dependencies and fixtures are named in its code. The short exercise in the Exercise tab is a separate standard-library practice.

```python
# Lesson program: audits workflow evidence, ordering, confidence, and friction.
# Lesson: phases/14-agent-engineering/48-discover-the-real-workflow/docs/en.md
# Canonical source: Nuseibeh and Easterbrook, Requirements Engineering: A Roadmap.
# Canonical source: Gotel and Finkelstein, ICRE 1994, DOI 10.1109/ICRE.1994.292398.
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evidence:
    source: str
    observation: str
    direct: bool
    confidence: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WorkflowStep:
    order: int
    actor: str
    action: str
    evidence: tuple[Evidence, ...]
    friction: str = ""


def audit(steps: list[WorkflowStep]) -> dict:
    orders = [step.order for step in steps]
    issues: list[str] = []
    if orders != list(range(1, len(steps) + 1)):
        issues.append("workflow order must be contiguous from one")
    for step in steps:
        if not step.evidence:
            issues.append(f"step {step.order} has no evidence")
        for item in step.evidence:
            if not 0 <= item.confidence <= 1:
                issues.append(f"step {step.order} has confidence outside zero to one")
    direct = sum(item.direct for step in steps for item in step.evidence)
    total = sum(len(step.evidence) for step in steps)
    return {
        "status": "grounded" if not issues and direct > 0 else "needs-evidence",
        "issues": issues,
        "direct_evidence_ratio": round(direct / total, 2) if total else 0,
        "friction_points": [step.friction for step in steps if step.friction],
        "steps": [asdict(step) for step in steps],
    }


def example() -> list[WorkflowStep]:
    return [
        WorkflowStep(1, "on-call engineer", "opens the alert", (Evidence("screen recording 01", "alert lacks service owner", True, 0.95),), "owner lookup"),
        WorkflowStep(2, "on-call engineer", "searches dashboards", (Evidence("incident 184", "three dashboards opened", True, 0.9),), "context switching"),
        WorkflowStep(3, "incident commander", "approves mitigation", (Evidence("runbook", "production writes require approval", False, 0.8),)),
    ]


def main() -> None:
    output = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "outputs" / "workflow-evidence.json"
    output.write_text(json.dumps(audit(example()), indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Apply it: Conduct discovery with evidence

## The engineering or business decision

Discovery is an investigation of how work actually happens. Ask for a recent concrete example, the steps performed, exception cases, review effort, and consequences of a mistake. Avoid leading questions that only confirm enthusiasm for AI. Capture what was observed separately from the client’s interpretation and your own assumptions.

If no real client is available, use the supplied fictional engagement scenario and role-play the interview. Do not present invented interview results as customer validation. A useful discovery record includes unanswered questions and a reason the project might not be suitable. Permission to discuss a workflow is not permission to copy or upload its documents.

## Worked example

Instead of “Would an AI summary save you time?”, ask “Walk me through the last handout you prepared. Which parts needed correction, who reviewed it, and how long did each step take?” A slow approval process may dominate the workflow, making faster generation a small part of the opportunity.

## Build it yourself

1. Write eight questions covering recent behavior, volume, inputs, errors, review, decision makers, and access constraints.
2. Run a role-play or a permissioned interview without recording by default.
3. Create an evidence table: observation, interpretation, assumption, unanswered question.
4. Identify a disconfirming observation that would make you decline or rescope the project.

## Break it deliberately

The client says the task happens daily, but the examples show only two cases last month. Preserve the discrepancy and request clarification instead of assuming a volume.

## Acceptance checks

- Interview notes distinguish actual observations from simulation.
- The dossier contains a recent end-to-end example.
- A reason to decline or change scope is explicit.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/discovery-dossier.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Separate interview evidence

### 1. Inspect the input and predict the outcome

Write down your decision before reading the walkthrough. Name the boundary, the relevant evidence, and the output that should be blocked or permitted.

```json
{
  "statement": "We do this every day",
  "observed_examples_last_month": 2
}
```

### 2. Work through the decision

A contradiction is a reason to clarify definitions, not to average guesses. Record the statement and observation separately.

The expected observation for this example is:

```json
{
  "volume": "unresolved",
  "next_question": "Which work was included in every day?"
}
```

### 3. Change an assumption

Use a role-play interview and label the entire record simulated.

### 4. Record your own experiment

Use the lesson-specific steps above to build or role-play the workflow. Record input revision, prediction, actual observation, discrepancy, decision and remaining uncertainty. In coding lessons, implement and run it in your own scratch environment. In client-delivery lessons, complete the named analysis or artifact. The academy saves written evidence; it does not run code or pretend to verify external work.

## Further experiments on these concepts

### Discover the Workflow People Actually Perform

1. Reconstruct one workflow from a log without interviewing anyone.
2. Interview a user and mark every claim that still lacks direct evidence.
3. Add one authority boundary and one failure-recovery step.
4. Model two workflow variants without merging them.
5. Identify a proposed feature that removes a visible step but leaves hidden work untouched.

chapters.title: Discovery interviews and evidence synthesis
chapters.body:
### Observe the work before proposing a solution
A discovery interview should reconstruct a recent completed case. Start with “Show me the last handout you prepared.” Ask which source arrived, how the operator decided what to include, which correction took longest, who approved it, and what happened after approval. Follow the artifact through the workflow. Asking whether AI would help invites a prediction; observing a recent correction gives you evidence.

### Use an interview sequence
Begin with context and permission. Move to a specific recent example. Trace its normal path. Ask for an exception and its consequence. Identify the people and systems involved. Finish by summarizing your understanding and asking what you missed. Keep questions neutral: “What happens when a note is incomplete?” gives more information than “Would automatic completion solve missing notes?” The latter hides the possibility that completing missing information is unacceptable.

### Keep an evidence ledger
Use four columns: observation, interpretation, assumption, and unresolved question. “The instructor corrected three objectives in the example” is an observation. “Objectives are the largest source of rework” is an interpretation requiring more examples. “This happens every week” is an assumption until you inspect records or hear a supported account. Write a source and date beside each observation. Mark role-play data as simulated.

### Resolve disagreement instead of averaging it
An operator says review takes ten minutes; a manager says two. Both can be describing different intervals. Ask each to identify start and end events. One may count source lookup while the other measures only approval clicks. Define a common timing rule, observe a case, and keep the disagreement in the record until resolved. Do not average incompatible measurements into a confident six-minute baseline.

### Handle access as a separate decision
Permission to discuss a document is not permission to upload it. Use a redacted or synthetic sample during initial discovery. Record who can authorize production access, which fields can leave the organization, and whether provider processing is permitted. If those answers are missing, your next deliverable may be a data-access map rather than a prototype.

### Interview exercise
Role-play an operator who wants faster drafts and an instructor whose main problem is factual errors. Ask eight questions without proposing a product. Produce a current-state map, three observations, two contradictions, one disconfirming finding, and a follow-up test. A good discovery summary can recommend no build when the bottleneck is approval ownership rather than text generation.

chapters.title: Discover the Workflow People Actually Perform
chapters.body:
## Start with the Current System

Do not begin by asking what features people want. Begin by reconstructing what happens now.

For each step, record:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Actor | On-call engineer |
| Trigger | Production alert arrives |
| Action | Opens alert, then searches dashboards |
| Input | Alert payload and deployment record |
| Output | Candidate service and owner |
| Friction | Context switching across three tools |
| Authority | Incident commander approves a write |
| Evidence | Screen recording, incident log, runbook |

The workflow is larger than the screen. It includes waiting, copy-paste, side channels, approval, error recovery, and the steps people have stopped noticing.

## Evidence Has Strength

Use a simple evidence ladder:

1. **Direct behavior:** observation, trace, recording, or system event.
2. **Artifact:** ticket, runbook, log, form, or completed output.
3. **Reported behavior:** a person describes what they do.
4. **Inference:** the team concludes what probably happens.

All four can be useful. Only the first two prove current behavior directly. Label the rest so confidence does not silently inflate.

**System flow**

- Trigger → Actor action
- Handoff
- Next actor action
- Outcome
- Direct evidence
- Artifact
- Reported behavior

## Search for Four Things

- **Friction:** repeated effort, delay, re-entry, or recovery.
- **Hidden state:** facts carried in memory, chat, or personal notes.
- **Authority:** the person or system allowed to make a consequential change.
- **Exceptions:** the case where the normal workflow stops being normal.

AI features often fail at handoffs and exceptions because the happy path was the only path shaped.

## Do Not Average Away Disagreement

Two users can perform different workflows for good reasons. Preserve the variants until you understand whether they represent:

- different roles;
- different risk levels;
- legacy and current process;
- expertise differences;
- a genuine policy disagreement.

An averaged workflow can describe nobody.

```python
# Lesson program: audits workflow evidence, ordering, confidence, and friction.
# Lesson: phases/14-agent-engineering/48-discover-the-real-workflow/docs/en.md
# Canonical source: Nuseibeh and Easterbrook, Requirements Engineering: A Roadmap.
# Canonical source: Gotel and Finkelstein, ICRE 1994, DOI 10.1109/ICRE.1994.292398.
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evidence:
    source: str
    observation: str
    direct: bool
    confidence: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WorkflowStep:
    order: int
    actor: str
    action: str
    evidence: tuple[Evidence, ...]
    friction: str = ""


def audit(steps: list[WorkflowStep]) -> dict:
    orders = [step.order for step in steps]
    issues: list[str] = []
    if orders != list(range(1, len(steps) + 1)):
        issues.append("workflow order must be contiguous from one")
    for step in steps:
        if not step.evidence:
            issues.append(f"step {step.order} has no evidence")
        for item in step.evidence:
            if not 0 <= item.confidence <= 1:
                issues.append(f"step {step.order} has confidence outside zero to one")
    direct = sum(item.direct for step in steps for item in step.evidence)
    total = sum(len(step.evidence) for step in steps)
    return {
        "status": "grounded" if not issues and direct > 0 else "needs-evidence",
        "issues": issues,
        "direct_evidence_ratio": round(direct / total, 2) if total else 0,
        "friction_points": [step.friction for step in steps if step.friction],
        "steps": [asdict(step) for step in steps],
    }


def example() -> list[WorkflowStep]:
    return [
        WorkflowStep(1, "on-call engineer", "opens the alert", (Evidence("screen recording 01", "alert lacks service owner", True, 0.95),), "owner lookup"),
        WorkflowStep(2, "on-call engineer", "searches dashboards", (Evidence("incident 184", "three dashboards opened", True, 0.9),), "context switching"),
        WorkflowStep(3, "incident commander", "approves mitigation", (Evidence("runbook", "production writes require approval", False, 0.8),)),
    ]


def main() -> None:
    output = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "outputs" / "workflow-evidence.json"
    output.write_text(json.dumps(audit(example()), indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

chapters.title: Apply it: Conduct discovery with evidence
chapters.body:
## The engineering or business decision

Discovery is an investigation of how work actually happens. Ask for a recent concrete example, the steps performed, exception cases, review effort, and consequences of a mistake. Avoid leading questions that only confirm enthusiasm for AI. Capture what was observed separately from the client’s interpretation and your own assumptions.

If no real client is available, use the supplied fictional engagement scenario and role-play the interview. Do not present invented interview results as customer validation. A useful discovery record includes unanswered questions and a reason the project might not be suitable. Permission to discuss a workflow is not permission to copy or upload its documents.

## Worked example

Instead of “Would an AI summary save you time?”, ask “Walk me through the last handout you prepared. Which parts needed correction, who reviewed it, and how long did each step take?” A slow approval process may dominate the workflow, making faster generation a small part of the opportunity.

## Build it yourself

1. Write eight questions covering recent behavior, volume, inputs, errors, review, decision makers, and access constraints.
2. Run a role-play or a permissioned interview without recording by default.
3. Create an evidence table: observation, interpretation, assumption, unanswered question.
4. Identify a disconfirming observation that would make you decline or rescope the project.

## Break it deliberately

The client says the task happens daily, but the examples show only two cases last month. Preserve the discrepancy and request clarification instead of assuming a volume.

## Acceptance checks

- Interview notes distinguish actual observations from simulation.
- The dossier contains a recent end-to-end example.
- A reason to decline or change scope is explicit.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/discovery-dossier.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

lessons.content:
# Measure the baseline and the decision value

## Baseline measurement and sensitivity analysis

### Specify the measurement contract
Define the unit, start event, stop event, sample selection, and exception policy before timing. For handouts, start when approved notes are available and stop when an instructor accepts a distributable draft. Include source lookup, correction, and rework. Measuring only model response time would omit most of the business workflow. Record individual cases rather than one remembered average.

### Calculate net benefit
Use an illustrative model: net monthly minutes = volume × (manual minutes − assisted preparation − assisted review − exception proportion × exception minutes) − monthly maintenance. The units must agree. If volume is 40, manual work 20, assisted preparation 4, review 10, exception proportion 0.2, exception work 15, and maintenance 30, the result is 40 × (20 − 4 − 10 − 3) − 30 = 90 minutes. It is not the 640 minutes implied by comparing manual work with generation alone.

### Distinguish capacity from cash
Ninety minutes returned to a salaried team is capacity, not automatically money saved. It may support faster response or additional work; it becomes a cash saving only under a separately justified staffing or expense change. Report time and financial assumptions separately. Do not multiply every saved minute by a billable rate and label the result profit.

### Stress the uncertain inputs
Run conservative, expected, and optimistic cases. Change review effort and exception rate first if those were unmeasured. With review at 14 minutes and exceptions at 30%, the same workflow can have negative benefit. That observation is useful: your pilot should measure review and exception cost before you promise scale. Use ranges to choose the next experiment, not to make a weak case look precise.

### Use paired comparisons carefully
Where possible, compare manual and assisted handling on comparable cases, with the same quality rubric. Avoid training the operator on every test case and then claiming general improvement. Keep some unseen cases for the final check. Report sample size, case mix, median time, range, and material failures. A small pilot guides a local decision; it does not establish universal productivity gains.

### Decision exercise
Build a table with ten synthetic cases, observed stages, error types, and acceptance outcomes. Calculate benefit after exceptions and maintenance. Identify the input at which benefit crosses zero. Write a stop rule such as “If more than two of ten drafts require reconstruction, investigate source quality before extending the pilot.” Explain the uncertainty that remains.

## Design Success Metrics Before the Result Exists

## Goal, Question, Metric

Start with a goal:

> Reduce time to identify the affected service without increasing unsafe actions.

Derive questions:

- How quickly is the correct service identified?
- How often is the identified service correct?
- Does diagnosis remain read-only?
- Does the workflow increase alert dismissal or operator workload?

Then choose metrics that operationalize those questions.

**System flow**

- Goal → Question about outcome
- Question about risk
- Outcome metric
- Guardrail metric
- Decision rule

## A Metric Needs a Contract

Every metric needs:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | `median_identification_seconds` |
| Direction | at most |
| Threshold | 120 |
| Window | ten incident replays |
| Source | replay event log |
| Population | on-call engineers in the pilot |
| Kind | outcome or guardrail |

Without source and window, a number cannot be reproduced. Without a threshold, it cannot drive a decision.

## Outcome, Guardrail, and Counter-Metric

- **Outcome metric:** did the desired state improve?
- **Guardrail:** did a fixed constraint remain true?
- **Counter-metric:** did the local improvement shift cost or harm elsewhere?

For an incident workflow, speed is not enough. Correctness, production writes, operator workload, and missed alerts protect against a fast but unsafe result.

## Offline and Online Evidence

Offline replay is useful for repeatability and edge coverage. A bounded pilot is useful for real behavior, trust, and workflow effects. Neither substitutes for the other.

Use the cheapest evidence that can answer the current decision. Do not expose real users merely because the implementation is ready.

## Decide Before You Measure

Write the pass, fail, and ambiguous paths before seeing results. Otherwise the team will move the threshold to protect the build.

Example:

- pass: correct service rate at least 0.9 and median time at most 120 seconds;
- fail: any production write or correct rate below 0.75;
- ambiguous: small improvement with wide variance, requiring a larger replay set.

## Design Success Metrics Before the Result Exists · implementation walkthrough

Read the control flow before running or changing it. This pinned teaching implementation illustrates the chapter; source-specific dependencies and fixtures are named in its code. The short exercise in the Exercise tab is a separate standard-library practice.

```python
# Lesson program for deriving reproducible metrics from outcome goals.
# Read: phases/14-agent-engineering/52-design-success-metrics/docs/en.md
# Reference: Basili, Software Modeling and Measurement: The GQM Paradigm, 1992.
# Reference: Basili, Caldiera, and Rombach, The Goal Question Metric Approach.
# Run this file to generate outputs/measurement-report.json.
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Metric:
    name: str
    direction: str
    threshold: float
    window: str
    source: str
    kind: str


@dataclass
class MeasurementPlan:
    goal: str
    questions: list[str]
    metrics: list[Metric]


def validate(plan: MeasurementPlan) -> list[str]:
    issues: list[str] = []
    if not plan.goal.strip():
        issues.append("goal is empty")
    if not plan.questions:
        issues.append("questions are empty")
    if not plan.metrics:
        issues.append("metrics are empty")
    kinds = {metric.kind for metric in plan.metrics}
    if "outcome" not in kinds:
        issues.append("outcome metric is missing")
    if "guardrail" not in kinds:
        issues.append("guardrail metric is missing")
    for metric in plan.metrics:
        if metric.direction not in {"at-most", "at-least"}:
            issues.append(f"{metric.name} has invalid direction")
        if not metric.source.strip() or not metric.window.strip():
            issues.append(f"{metric.name} lacks source or window")
    return issues


def evaluate(metric: Metric, value: float) -> bool:
    if metric.direction == "at-most":
        return value <= metric.threshold
    if metric.direction == "at-least":
        return value >= metric.threshold
    raise ValueError("invalid direction")


def report(plan: MeasurementPlan, values: dict[str, float]) -> dict:
    issues = validate(plan)
    results = []
    for metric in plan.metrics:
        if metric.direction not in {"at-most", "at-least"}:
            result = {"name": metric.name, "status": "invalid"}
            if metric.name in values:
                result["value"] = values[metric.name]
            results.append(result)
        elif metric.name not in values:
            results.append({"name": metric.name, "status": "missing"})
        else:
            results.append({"name": metric.name, "value": values[metric.name], "passed": evaluate(metric, values[metric.name])})
    return {"status": "valid" if not issues else "invalid", "issues": issues, "plan": asdict(plan), "results": results}


def example() -> MeasurementPlan:
    return MeasurementPlan(
        goal="Reduce time to identify the affected service without increasing unsafe actions",
        questions=["How quickly is the correct service identified?", "Does diagnosis remain read-only?"],
        metrics=[
            Metric("median_identification_seconds", "at-most", 120, "ten incident replays", "replay log", "outcome"),
            Metric("correct_service_rate", "at-least", 0.9, "ten incident replays", "incident record", "outcome"),
            Metric("production_writes", "at-most", 0, "entire pilot", "audit log", "guardrail"),
        ],
    )


def main() -> None:
    values = {"median_identification_seconds": 94, "correct_service_rate": 0.9, "production_writes": 0}
    output = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "outputs" / "measurement-report.json"
    output.write_text(json.dumps(report(example(), values), indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## FinOps for LLMs — Unit Economics and Multi-Tenant Attribution

## The Problem

Your bill says $40,000. You don't know:
- Which tenant spent it.
- Which product feature drove it.
- Whether any individual user was abusive.
- Whether prompt bloat, tool calls, or memory amplification was the culprit.

Tag-and-aggregate on provider-side works for cloud resources (EC2, S3) where tags propagate to line items. LLM API calls do not auto-tag — you have to stamp user/task/tenant at the call site and carry through. Retroactive attribution always misses edge cases.

## The Concept

### Three attribution dimensions

**Per-user** (`user_id`): who is costing what. Drives seat pricing, expansion conversations, identifies power users.

**Per-task** (`task_id` + `route`): which product surface costs what. Drives feature prioritization, kill-expensive-features decisions.

**Per-tenant** (`tenant_id`): which customer is profitable. Drives unit economics, renewal pricing, tier thresholds.

Instrument all three at call site on day one. Retroactive is always worse.

### Four token layers

| Layer | Example | Typical % of total |
|-------|---------|---------------------|
| Prompt | system + user input | 40-60% |
| Tool | tool-call results fed back | 20-40% (agent workloads) |
| Memory | prior conversation / retrieved docs | 10-30% |
| Response | model output | 10-30% |

Bucketing all four together makes optimization blind. Break them out in your attribution schema.

### Enforcement ladder

1. **Rate limit** per tenant. 2-3x expected peak. Return 429 with `Retry-After`. Tenant sees friction; no surprise bill.

2. **Daily spend cap** per tenant. 1.5-3x contracted ceiling. Trigger: tighten rate limit + alert customer-success.

3. **Kill switch** on spend z-score > 4 relative to tenant baseline. Auto-pause tenant; page on-call; escalate to ops + CS.

### Attribution patterns

- **Tag-and-aggregate**: stamp metadata headers; aggregate later. Simple; rough.
- **Telemetry joiner**: join traces to billing via trace IDs. Highest accuracy. What mature teams do.
- **Sampling + extrapolation**: sample 5-10%, multiply. Cost-effective for rough spend; misses tails.
- **Model-based allocation**: regression to infer cost driver. For legacy data without tags.
- **Event-sourced**: cost as events in a stream (Kafka / Kinesis). Real-time.
- **Real-time streaming**: dashboard updates sub-second.

### Cost per X is the unit metric

$/M tokens is vendor speak. Product metrics:

- Cost per resolved support ticket.
- Cost per generated article.
- Cost per successful agent task.
- Cost per user-session-minute.

Tie cost to a product outcome. Otherwise optimization is unanchored.

### Cost attribution trace shape

```
trace_id: abc123
  user_id: u_42
  tenant_id: t_7
  task_id: task_classify_doc
  route: model_haiku
  layers:
    prompt_tokens: 1800
    tool_tokens: 600
    memory_tokens: 400
    response_tokens: 150
  cost_usd: 0.0135
  cached_input: true
  batch: false
```

Emit on every call. Store in data lake. Aggregate per dimension. the related topic observability stack is where this lives.

### The compounded-savings stack

Stack: cache + batch + route + gateway. With all four:
- Cache L2 (the related topic): ~10x cheaper input.
- Batch (the related topic): 50% off.
- Route to cheap model (the related topic): 60% cost reduction.
- Gateway efficiency (the related topic): redundancy + retries.

Best-case stacked: ~5-10% of naive baseline. Most teams have 2-3 levers engaged; few stack all four.

## Apply it: Measure the baseline and the decision value

## The engineering or business decision

A business case should count the work that remains after automation. Measure preparation, generation, correction, approval, and exception handling separately. Time saved is only one possible outcome: consistency, turnaround, accessibility, or traceability may matter more. State the denominator and uncertainty in any estimate.

Use a range rather than a single optimistic forecast. Do not assume every generated output is usable or every saved minute becomes cash. A pilot should test the most important uncertain assumption. Choose measures that you can observe in a small engagement and that the buyer agrees are relevant.

## Worked example

A fictional team handles 40 documents per month. Manual preparation takes 12 minutes and review takes eight. A prototype reduces preparation to four minutes but increases review to ten. The net reduction is six minutes per document, or four hours at that volume, before support and exception work. This is an illustrative calculation, not a promised result.

## Build it yourself

1. Create a baseline sheet for at least five synthetic or permissioned examples.
2. Separate preparation, review, rework, and exception time.
3. Model conservative, expected, and optimistic scenarios using editable assumptions.
4. Choose a pilot success measure and an explicit condition for stopping.

## Break it deliberately

Increase exception rate and review time in the model. Check whether the project still has a useful benefit and explain the change.

## Acceptance checks

- The model includes review and maintenance effort.
- Every estimate has a source or an assumption label.
- The pilot tests a material uncertainty.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/baseline-model.csv`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

exercise.material:
## Include the work automation leaves behind

### 1. Inspect the input and predict the outcome

Write down your decision before reading the walkthrough. Name the boundary, the relevant evidence, and the output that should be blocked or permitted.

```json
{
  "volume": 40,
  "manual_minutes": 20,
  "assisted_prepare": 4,
  "review": 10,
  "exception_rate": 0.2,
  "exception_minutes": 15,
  "maintenance_minutes": 30
}
```

### 2. Work through the decision

The net benefit includes review, exception handling and maintenance. Time returned is capacity, not automatically a cash saving.

The expected observation for this example is:

```json
{
  "net_monthly_minutes": 90
}
```

### 3. Change an assumption

Raise review to 14 and exception rate to 0.3; explain the negative result before proposing expansion.

### 4. Record your own experiment

Use the lesson-specific steps above to build or role-play the workflow. Record input revision, prediction, actual observation, discrepancy, decision and remaining uncertainty. In coding lessons, implement and run it in your own scratch environment. In client-delivery lessons, complete the named analysis or artifact. The academy saves written evidence; it does not run code or pretend to verify external work.

## Coding experiment: Workflow benefit calculation

The function includes assisted review and exception work but excludes monthly maintenance; subtract maintenance separately. A negative result is evidence to investigate or stop, not a number to hide.

### Behavioral checks

```python
assert net_minutes(40, 20, 4, 10, 0.2, 15) == 120
assert net_minutes(40, 20, 4, 14, 0.3, 15) == -100
```

### Starter to implement

```python
def net_minutes(volume, manual, assisted, review, exceptions, exception_minutes):
    """Net monthly minutes; exceptions is a proportion between zero and one."""
    raise NotImplementedError('Implement workflow economics')
```

### Reference implementation to explain and extend

```python
import re
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation

def net_minutes(volume,manual,assisted,review,exceptions,exception_minutes):
    numbers=[volume,manual,assisted,review,exceptions,exception_minutes]
    if any(isinstance(n,bool) or not isinstance(n,(int,float)) or not __import__('math').isfinite(n) or n<0 for n in numbers) or exceptions>1:
        raise ValueError('nonnegative finite values and an exception proportion are required')
    return volume*(manual-assisted-review-exceptions*exception_minutes)
```

## Further experiments on these concepts

### Design Success Metrics Before the Result Exists

1. Derive three questions from one outcome goal.
2. Add a counter-metric that catches cost shifted to another role.
3. Define the source, population, and window for every metric.
4. Write pass, fail, and ambiguous decisions before generating values.
5. Identify one metric that is easy to collect but cannot change the decision. Remove it.

### FinOps for LLMs — Unit Economics and Multi-Tenant Attribution

1. Run `code/main.py`. At what z-score does the kill switch fire? How do you pick the threshold?
2. Design a per-tenant, per-task cost dashboard. What are the 5 views you build first?
3. Your largest tenant is unit-economics-negative. Propose three interventions ordered by customer impact.
4. Compute cost per resolved ticket for a support product: 3M tokens/ticket, ~800 tickets/day, GPT-5 cached rate.
5. Argue whether retroactive tagging can ever work. When is it acceptable?

chapters.title: Baseline measurement and sensitivity analysis
chapters.body:
### Specify the measurement contract
Define the unit, start event, stop event, sample selection, and exception policy before timing. For handouts, start when approved notes are available and stop when an instructor accepts a distributable draft. Include source lookup, correction, and rework. Measuring only model response time would omit most of the business workflow. Record individual cases rather than one remembered average.

### Calculate net benefit
Use an illustrative model: net monthly minutes = volume × (manual minutes − assisted preparation − assisted review − exception proportion × exception minutes) − monthly maintenance. The units must agree. If volume is 40, manual work 20, assisted preparation 4, review 10, exception proportion 0.2, exception work 15, and maintenance 30, the result is 40 × (20 − 4 − 10 − 3) − 30 = 90 minutes. It is not the 640 minutes implied by comparing manual work with generation alone.

### Distinguish capacity from cash
Ninety minutes returned to a salaried team is capacity, not automatically money saved. It may support faster response or additional work; it becomes a cash saving only under a separately justified staffing or expense change. Report time and financial assumptions separately. Do not multiply every saved minute by a billable rate and label the result profit.

### Stress the uncertain inputs
Run conservative, expected, and optimistic cases. Change review effort and exception rate first if those were unmeasured. With review at 14 minutes and exceptions at 30%, the same workflow can have negative benefit. That observation is useful: your pilot should measure review and exception cost before you promise scale. Use ranges to choose the next experiment, not to make a weak case look precise.

### Use paired comparisons carefully
Where possible, compare manual and assisted handling on comparable cases, with the same quality rubric. Avoid training the operator on every test case and then claiming general improvement. Keep some unseen cases for the final check. Report sample size, case mix, median time, range, and material failures. A small pilot guides a local decision; it does not establish universal productivity gains.

### Decision exercise
Build a table with ten synthetic cases, observed stages, error types, and acceptance outcomes. Calculate benefit after exceptions and maintenance. Identify the input at which benefit crosses zero. Write a stop rule such as “If more than two of ten drafts require reconstruction, investigate source quality before extending the pilot.” Explain the uncertainty that remains.

chapters.title: Design Success Metrics Before the Result Exists
chapters.body:
## Goal, Question, Metric

Start with a goal:

> Reduce time to identify the affected service without increasing unsafe actions.

Derive questions:

- How quickly is the correct service identified?
- How often is the identified service correct?
- Does diagnosis remain read-only?
- Does the workflow increase alert dismissal or operator workload?

Then choose metrics that operationalize those questions.

**System flow**

- Goal → Question about outcome
- Question about risk
- Outcome metric
- Guardrail metric
- Decision rule

## A Metric Needs a Contract

Every metric needs:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | `median_identification_seconds` |
| Direction | at most |
| Threshold | 120 |
| Window | ten incident replays |
| Source | replay event log |
| Population | on-call engineers in the pilot |
| Kind | outcome or guardrail |

Without source and window, a number cannot be reproduced. Without a threshold, it cannot drive a decision.

## Outcome, Guardrail, and Counter-Metric

- **Outcome metric:** did the desired state improve?
- **Guardrail:** did a fixed constraint remain true?
- **Counter-metric:** did the local improvement shift cost or harm elsewhere?

For an incident workflow, speed is not enough. Correctness, production writes, operator workload, and missed alerts protect against a fast but unsafe result.

## Offline and Online Evidence

Offline replay is useful for repeatability and edge coverage. A bounded pilot is useful for real behavior, trust, and workflow effects. Neither substitutes for the other.

Use the cheapest evidence that can answer the current decision. Do not expose real users merely because the implementation is ready.

## Decide Before You Measure

Write the pass, fail, and ambiguous paths before seeing results. Otherwise the team will move the threshold to protect the build.

Example:

- pass: correct service rate at least 0.9 and median time at most 120 seconds;
- fail: any production write or correct rate below 0.75;
- ambiguous: small improvement with wide variance, requiring a larger replay set.

chapters.body:
## The Problem

Your bill says $40,000. You don't know:
- Which tenant spent it.
- Which product feature drove it.
- Whether any individual user was abusive.
- Whether prompt bloat, tool calls, or memory amplification was the culprit.

Tag-and-aggregate on provider-side works for cloud resources (EC2, S3) where tags propagate to line items. LLM API calls do not auto-tag — you have to stamp user/task/tenant at the call site and carry through. Retroactive attribution always misses edge cases.

## The Concept

### Three attribution dimensions

**Per-user** (`user_id`): who is costing what. Drives seat pricing, expansion conversations, identifies power users.

**Per-task** (`task_id` + `route`): which product surface costs what. Drives feature prioritization, kill-expensive-features decisions.

**Per-tenant** (`tenant_id`): which customer is profitable. Drives unit economics, renewal pricing, tier thresholds.

Instrument all three at call site on day one. Retroactive is always worse.

### Four token layers

| Layer | Example | Typical % of total |
|-------|---------|---------------------|
| Prompt | system + user input | 40-60% |
| Tool | tool-call results fed back | 20-40% (agent workloads) |
| Memory | prior conversation / retrieved docs | 10-30% |
| Response | model output | 10-30% |

Bucketing all four together makes optimization blind. Break them out in your attribution schema.

### Enforcement ladder

1. **Rate limit** per tenant. 2-3x expected peak. Return 429 with `Retry-After`. Tenant sees friction; no surprise bill.

2. **Daily spend cap** per tenant. 1.5-3x contracted ceiling. Trigger: tighten rate limit + alert customer-success.

3. **Kill switch** on spend z-score > 4 relative to tenant baseline. Auto-pause tenant; page on-call; escalate to ops + CS.

### Attribution patterns

- **Tag-and-aggregate**: stamp metadata headers; aggregate later. Simple; rough.
- **Telemetry joiner**: join traces to billing via trace IDs. Highest accuracy. What mature teams do.
- **Sampling + extrapolation**: sample 5-10%, multiply. Cost-effective for rough spend; misses tails.
- **Model-based allocation**: regression to infer cost driver. For legacy data without tags.
- **Event-sourced**: cost as events in a stream (Kafka / Kinesis). Real-time.
- **Real-time streaming**: dashboard updates sub-second.

### Cost per X is the unit metric

$/M tokens is vendor speak. Product metrics:

- Cost per resolved support ticket.
- Cost per generated article.
- Cost per successful agent task.
- Cost per user-session-minute.

Tie cost to a product outcome. Otherwise optimization is unanchored.

### Cost attribution trace shape

```
trace_id: abc123
  user_id: u_42
  tenant_id: t_7
  task_id: task_classify_doc
  route: model_haiku
  layers:
    prompt_tokens: 1800
    tool_tokens: 600
    memory_tokens: 400
    response_tokens: 150
  cost_usd: 0.0135
  cached_input: true
  batch: false
```

Emit on every call. Store in data lake. Aggregate per dimension. the related topic observability stack is where this lives.

### The compounded-savings stack

Stack: cache + batch + route + gateway. With all four:
- Cache L2 (the related topic): ~10x cheaper input.
- Batch (the related topic): 50% off.
- Route to cheap model (the related topic): 60% cost reduction.
- Gateway efficiency (the related topic): redundancy + retries.

Best-case stacked: ~5-10% of naive baseline. Most teams have 2-3 levers engaged; few stack all four.

chapters.title: Apply it: Measure the baseline and the decision value
chapters.body:
## The engineering or business decision

A business case should count the work that remains after automation. Measure preparation, generation, correction, approval, and exception handling separately. Time saved is only one possible outcome: consistency, turnaround, accessibility, or traceability may matter more. State the denominator and uncertainty in any estimate.

Use a range rather than a single optimistic forecast. Do not assume every generated output is usable or every saved minute becomes cash. A pilot should test the most important uncertain assumption. Choose measures that you can observe in a small engagement and that the buyer agrees are relevant.

## Worked example

A fictional team handles 40 documents per month. Manual preparation takes 12 minutes and review takes eight. A prototype reduces preparation to four minutes but increases review to ten. The net reduction is six minutes per document, or four hours at that volume, before support and exception work. This is an illustrative calculation, not a promised result.

## Build it yourself

1. Create a baseline sheet for at least five synthetic or permissioned examples.
2. Separate preparation, review, rework, and exception time.
3. Model conservative, expected, and optimistic scenarios using editable assumptions.
4. Choose a pilot success measure and an explicit condition for stopping.

## Break it deliberately

Increase exception rate and review time in the model. Check whether the project still has a useful benefit and explain the change.

## Acceptance checks

- The model includes review and maintenance effort.
- Every estimate has a source or an assumption label.
- The pilot tests a material uncertainty.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/baseline-model.csv`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

lessons.content:
# Package a service with a bounded outcome

## Service packaging and staged commitments

### Package a decision, not an unlimited capability
A diagnostic, a pilot, and production support answer different questions. A diagnostic identifies the workflow and feasibility. A pilot tests a bounded change with named users and representative inputs. Production requires ownership, access controls, monitoring, support, and recovery. Give each stage its own deliverable and decision gate. A successful diagnostic does not silently authorize production use.

### Build a service boundary
Describe supported input formats, volume, roles, output, review duty, and exclusions. For example, the handout pilot accepts approved UTF-8 course notes in one template, produces draft handouts with source IDs, and requires instructor approval. It excludes scanned documents, new curriculum creation, automated distribution, and confidential learner data. Exclusions are useful when they prevent a buyer from inferring a capability you have not tested.

### Make dependencies visible
List what the client must provide: representative samples, a reviewer, access decisions, a test environment, and an acceptance owner. Attach a date and consequence to each dependency. If approved samples arrive late, the evaluation schedule changes. Avoid a fixed delivery date that assumes inputs you do not control. A dependency table makes negotiation about the actual work possible.

### Offer useful alternatives
If the source material is inconsistent, offer a data-readiness diagnostic before implementation. If the buyer cannot assign a reviewer, offer a read-only search tool rather than a drafting workflow that needs review. Alternatives should preserve the desired outcome while changing the operational burden. They should not be arbitrary tiers that differ only in the number of prompts.

### Test the offer with teach-back
Give the one-page service description to a reviewer and ask: What will you receive? What can it do with incomplete notes? Who approves a draft? What costs recur? What happens when it fails? Any mismatch between their answers and your intent is a specification defect. Revise the offer before treating agreement as informed.

### Packaging exercise
Write diagnostic, pilot, and expansion cards. Each needs a decision question, inputs, outputs, exclusions, client duties, acceptance evidence, and stop condition. Use fictional costs if practicing. No card should guarantee an income, accuracy rate, or saving that has not been measured.

## Choose the Smallest Slice That Can Change the Decision

## Vertical Means Evidence End to End

A useful slice crosses the minimum real workflow needed to observe an outcome. It can be narrow in users, data, duration, and capability. It should not be narrow by removing the exact uncertainty you need to test.

Examples:

- A read-only replay across ten real incidents tests service identification and operator trust.
- A polished dashboard on synthetic data may test comprehension but not data feasibility.
- A production auto-remediator tests everything at once with unacceptable consequence.

## Define Required Proof First

Take the highest-risk open assumptions and turn them into a required proof set. A candidate slice is eligible only if it covers that set.

Then compare eligible slices on:

| Dimension | Direction |
|---|---|
| Outcome value | More is better |
| Uncertainty reduced | More is better |
| Effort | Less is better |
| Consequence | Less is better |
| Reversibility | More is better |

The lab’s score is intentionally simple. The eligibility gate matters more than the arithmetic.

**System flow**

- Required proof → Candidate slice 1
- Candidate slice 2
- Candidate slice 3
- Reject
- Compare evidence per effort and risk
- Build one slice

## Common False Minimums

- **The UI-only minimum:** removes the data and operational uncertainty.
- **The infrastructure-only minimum:** proves technical possibility without user value.
- **The happy-path minimum:** omits the exception that creates most risk.
- **The demo minimum:** produces a persuasive artifact but no repeatable measurement.
- **The platform minimum:** builds reusable machinery before one workflow earns it.

## Add a Stop Rule

Before implementation, write what happens if the slice fails:

- abandon the outcome;
- change the target user or situation;
- test a different mechanism;
- collect better evidence;
- narrow authority further.

If every result leads to “keep building,” the slice is not an experiment.

## Choose Prototype, Pilot, or Production Deliberately

## Three Different Questions

| Stage | Primary question |
|---|---|
| Prototype | Can this mechanism produce the evidence at all? |
| Pilot | Does it work safely with a bounded real audience and real conditions? |
| Production | Can we own it continuously at the promised reliability and risk level? |

A prototype can be technically complete and still be disposable. A pilot can use production data while remaining limited in audience and authority. Production begins when the organization accepts ongoing responsibility.

## Prototype

Use a prototype when the unknown does not require real users or real data. Keep it:

- discardable;
- isolated;
- narrow in behavior;
- explicit about the learning question;
- free of false operational guarantees.

Do not optimize architecture before the mechanism earns another stage.

## Pilot

Use a pilot when the unknown requires real behavior, realistic data, or a real workflow, but consequence or readiness is not yet compatible with broad release.

A pilot needs:

- a named audience;
- a human owner;
- bounded duration and authority;
- audit and rollback;
- outcome and guardrail thresholds;
- exit criteria for expand, revise, or stop.

## Production

Production needs more than deployment:

- service level objective;
- on-call and incident ownership;
- security and privacy review;
- cost and capacity controls;
- rollback and recovery;
- continuous monitoring;
- a retirement path.

**System flow**

- Unknown
- Prototype
- Pilot
- Production

## Stage Drift

Prototype code becomes dangerous when it acquires users, data, or authority without acquiring ownership. Mark prototype and pilot boundaries in configuration, access control, telemetry, and documentation. A warning banner is not enough.

The stage should be observable from the system itself.

## Apply it: Package a service with a bounded outcome

## The engineering or business decision

A well-scoped service describes deliverables, supported inputs, exclusions, dependencies, and acceptance. It should be understandable without knowing which model or framework you use. Package a diagnostic, a pilot, and a possible expansion separately so the client can make a decision after seeing evidence.

Your offer must align with what you can support. If you have only tested plain English text, do not include arbitrary PDFs, scans, voice notes, and multilingual documents under “document automation.” Make the reviewer’s role and the manual fallback visible. A bounded promise is more credible and easier to price than an open-ended commitment to improve everything.

## Worked example

Pilot: “Draft participant handouts from one approved course template, with source references and instructor review.” Inputs: up to 20 synthetic text notes for testing. Exclusions: public publishing, automatic email, scanned PDFs, and changes to approved curriculum. Deliverables: prototype, evaluation report, and handover instructions.

## Build it yourself

1. Write a one-page service offer for the simulated client.
2. Define supported input formats, volume, users, review step, and output.
3. List at least five exclusions that prevent ambiguous expectations.
4. Describe the evidence required before offering an expanded engagement.

## Break it deliberately

The buyer assumes the pilot includes writing new curriculum and sending it to students. Revise the offer so those effects cannot be mistaken for included work.

## Acceptance checks

- The offer describes an outcome and tangible artifacts.
- Input boundaries and review duties are explicit.
- Expansion requires a separate decision.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-02/service-offer.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

exercise.material:
## Package a bounded pilot

### 1. Inspect the input and predict the outcome

Write down your decision before reading the walkthrough. Name the boundary, the relevant evidence, and the output that should be blocked or permitted.

```json
{
  "input": "approved text notes",
  "output": "reviewed handout",
  "requested_extra": "automatic distribution"
}
```

### 2. Work through the decision

A service boundary is a promise about behavior, not a list of tools. Keep source, review and external actions explicit.

The expected observation for this example is:

```json
{
  "included": "draft and review",
  "excluded": "sending",
  "expansion_gate": "separate effect design and acceptance"
}
```

### 3. Change an assumption

Add scanned input and identify the new feasibility evidence required.

### 4. Record your own experiment

Use the lesson-specific steps above to build or role-play the workflow. Record input revision, prediction, actual observation, discrepancy, decision and remaining uncertainty. In coding lessons, implement and run it in your own scratch environment. In client-delivery lessons, complete the named analysis or artifact. The academy saves written evidence; it does not run code or pretend to verify external work.

## Further experiments on these concepts

### Choose the Smallest Slice That Can Change the Decision

1. Design three slices for the same outcome at different consequence levels.
2. State the required proof set before scoring them.
3. Remove one capability while preserving the decisive evidence.
4. Add a stop rule for a failed pilot.
5. Identify a reusable platform component that should wait until after the slice.

### Choose Prototype, Pilot, or Production Deliberately

1. Classify three current projects by learning stage, not deployment status.
2. Write pilot exit criteria that include a stop decision.
3. Add a technical control that prevents a prototype from reaching production data.
4. Identify the first operational responsibility that makes the build production.
5. Design a rollback receipt for the bounded pilot.
